titre: The Naked Mole-Rat, a Longevity Anomaly
accroche: On the graph linking a mammal's size to its lifespan, this mouse-sized animal ranks alongside the human species.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1981, biologist Jennifer Jarvis publishes in Science the study of a colony of 40 naked mole-rats captured in southern Africa, and describes a way of life never before documented in a mammal. Only one female in the colony breeds; the rest of the individuals divide into castes distinguished by size and task, with overlapping generations and cooperative care of the young. This organization, until then reserved in biologists' vocabulary for ants, termites, and a few bees, has since earned the naked mole-rat its billing as one of the few eusocial mammals. The term remains debated: the criteria designed for social insects do not exactly cover this animal's organization, and whether or not to call it “eusocial” depends mostly on the definition one adopts.

## A Longevity Anomaly, Actively Debated

This same mouse-sized animal lives remarkably long: Rochelle Buffenstein and Jennifer Jarvis describe it, in 2002, as an outlier on the graph linking a mammal's body mass to its longevity, in the same category as Homo sapiens. Individuals exceed 30 years in captivity.

In 2018, a team led by Buffenstein goes further: analyzing more than 3,000 survival records, it detects no rise in mortality risk with age, even in animals that had passed 25 times the age of their reproductive maturity: an exception to the Gompertz law, which describes an exponential rise in the risk of death with age in virtually all mammals studied. The result has since been challenged: a critique published in 2019 points out that 87% of the animals followed were followed for only eight years or less, and that fewer than 1% were observed beyond 18 years, too few to settle what really happens at advanced ages. The question remains open.

## Resistant, Not Immune

The naked mole-rat's reputation also includes a near-total resistance to cancer, widely relayed in the press. A 2021 review corrects the formula: cases of cancer do exist in the species, but their frequency remains exceptionally low compared with other mammals of similar size, humans included. The cellular mechanism long put forward to explain it (early contact inhibition, which would make naked mole-rat cells stop dividing in culture at a much lower density than in other rodents) is in fact much less solid than advertised: the same review notes that the phenomenon depends heavily on culture conditions, and that under other conditions (regular changes of medium), the cells reach high density with no sign of contact inhibition. What the relative resistance to cancer owes to this specific cellular mechanism therefore remains to be established.

What the solid data tell (an animal far outside the norm on the longevity curve, a mortality that does not climb clearly with age over the well-documented period, a cancer that is rare without being absent) is more than enough in itself, with no need to round up toward immortality to make the animal interesting.

repere.texte: Across more than 3,000 survival records analyzed, naked mole-rats' mortality risk does not increase with age, even 25 times beyond their reproductive maturity: an exception to the Gompertz law that governs aging in nearly all mammals studied.
repere.source: Ruby, Smith & Buffenstein, “Naked mole-rat mortality rates defy Gompertzian laws by not increasing with age,” eLife, 2018

carte.punch: A mouse-sized rodent ranks, on the longevity curve, alongside humans.
carte.idee: The naked mole-rat lives in colonies where only one female breeds, an organization until then reserved for social insects. It also lives remarkably long and rarely develops cancer. Its reputation for total immortality, though, goes beyond what the data establish.
carte.source_courte: Jarvis, Science, 1981; Ruby et al., eLife, 2018

quiz.question: What does the 2021 review correct about the naked mole-rat's resistance to cancer?
choix: That not a single case of cancer has ever been recorded in this species, contrary to a common belief
That cases of cancer do exist in the species, but remain exceptionally rare compared with other mammals of similar size
That the naked mole-rat actually develops more cancers than the laboratory mouse
That resistance to cancer has never been observed outside captive breeding colonies
quiz.explication: The widely relayed reputation for total immunity to cancer is inaccurate: cases exist in the naked mole-rat, but their frequency remains far below that seen in mammals of comparable size, humans included. The resistance is therefore relative, not absolute.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Jennifer Jarvis's study, published in Science in 1981, describe?
choix: A colony of 40 naked mole-rats in which only one female breeds, organized into castes
A laboratory experiment measuring the species' resistance to cancer
The first direct measurement of the naked mole-rat's maximum longevity
A cross between naked mole-rats and ordinary laboratory rats
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card specifies that Jarvis publishes in 1981 the study of a colony of 40 naked mole-rats, describing a way of life new to a mammal: a single breeding female, castes by size and task, overlapping generations.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do Buffenstein and Jarvis describe the naked mole-rat, in 2002, on the graph linking body mass and longevity?
choix: As a case perfectly in line with the general trend among rodents
As the shortest-lived rodent species ever recorded
As an outlier, in the same category as the human species
As a case too rare to be plotted on such a graph
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card states that Buffenstein and Jarvis describe, in 2002, the naked mole-rat as an outlier on the body mass/longevity graph, in the same category as Homo sapiens, despite its size comparable to a mouse's.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 2018 study by Rochelle Buffenstein's team find, from more than 3,000 survival records?
choix: An exponential rise in mortality risk consistent with the Gompertz law
No detectable rise in mortality risk with age, even well beyond reproductive maturity
A sharp drop in mortality after reproductive maturity, never seen elsewhere
A rise in mortality risk twice as fast as in the laboratory mouse
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card reports that the 2018 study detects no rise in mortality risk with age, even in animals that had passed 25 times the age of their reproductive maturity, an exception to the Gompertz law.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the critique published in 2019 point out about the data of the 2018 study?
choix: That the data had been collected on sick animals, skewing the results
That the 2018 study had never been reviewed by other researchers before publication
That all the naked mole-rats studied came from one and the same captive colony
That 87% of the animals followed were followed for only eight years or less, too few to settle the question at advanced ages
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card cites this 2019 critique precisely: 87% of the animals followed were followed for only eight years or less, and fewer than 1% were observed beyond 18 years, judged insufficient to settle what happens at advanced ages.
